Packing Diverse Short Cycles

**Abstract**

Bentert, Fomin, Golovach, Korhonen, Lochet, Panolan, Ramanujan, Saurabh, and Simonov (SODA 2025) initiated the parameterized study of Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing: given a weighted graph _G_ and an integer _k_, decide whether _G_ contains _k_ edge-disjoint cycles of minimum weight. They showed that the problem admits an algorithm running in time _n_<sup>O(_k_<sup>6</sup>)</sup> and asked whether it is fixed-parameter tractable or W[1]-hard parameterized by _k_. We resolve this question by proving that Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing is W[1]-hard parameterized by _k_, even on unweighted subcubic graphs. The same lower bound also applies to the vertex-disjoint variant.

For planar graphs, the same paper provides a construction of a kernel with O(_k_<sup>2</sup>) vertices and an algorithm running in time \(k^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\), and explicitly asked whether the problem admits a single-exponential algorithm of running time \(2^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\). Rather than addressing this question in isolation, we introduce a more general framework, Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage, which asks for _k_ shortest cycles that may overlap in a controlled way while maximizing the total weight of covered edges. This framework simultaneously captures edge-disjoint shortest cycle packing, the problem of finding diverse shortest cycles, and the problem of maximizing edge coverage by shortest cycles. Our main algorithmic result shows that Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage can be solved on planar graphs in time \(2^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\), thereby establishing a single-exponential algorithm for Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing as a special case.

The key ingredient behind our algorithm is a structural analysis of the _Laminar Shortest Cycles Tree_, a tree-like decomposition that reveals a laminar interaction pattern among shortest cycles in planar graphs and enables an efficient dynamic programming algorithm.

## 1 Introduction

Cycle packing is a fundamental optimization problem in which one seeks to find the maximum number of edge- (or vertex-) disjoint cycles in a graph. The authors in \[4, 3\] initiated the study of Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing and Vertex-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing, the problems where one seeks a packing of _k_ shortest (minimum-weight) edge- (or vertex-) disjoint cycles, respectively. They showed that both packing problems are solvable in time _n_<sup>O(_k_<sup>6</sup>)</sup>, while ruling out a kernel of size polynomial in _k_ under standard complexity assumptions. Our first theorem resolves the FPT vs. W\[1\]-hard question left open in \[3\].

**Theorem 1.1.** Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing _is W\[1\]-hard parameterized by k on unweighted subcubic graphs._

Since two cycles in a subcubic graph are edge-disjoint if and only if they are vertex-disjoint, we immediately obtain the hardness for the vertex-disjoint variant of the problem.

**Corollary 1.1.** Vertex-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing _is W\[1\]-hard parameterized by k on unweighted subcubic graphs._

Theorem 1.1 rules out fixed-parameter tractability under standard assumptions for general graphs. For planar graphs, the authors in \[4, 3\] showed that Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing admits a kernel with O(_k_<sup>2</sup>) vertices and an algorithm running in time \(k^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\), and asked explicitly whether a _single-exponential_ algorithm with running time \(2^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\) exists.

Our next theorem resolves a more general question than what was asked in \[3\]. It works for a natural relaxation of edge-disjointness: for an integer \(d\ge 0\), two cycles _C_<sub>1</sub> and _C_<sub>2</sub> are _d-diverse_ if \(w(E(C_1)\cap E(C_2))\le d\), that is, the total weight of shared edges is at most _d_. Edge-disjointness is the special case _d_=0. Building on this, we introduce the following problem, which simultaneously captures edge-disjoint shortest cycle packing, the search for diverse shortest cycles, and the problem of maximizing edge coverage by shortest cycles.

The framework of Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage captures several problems of independent interest.

• **Edge-disjoint Packing.** Taking _d_=0 (or equivalently \(\ell=k\cdot g(G)\)) forces the _k_ cycles to be pairwise edge-disjoint, recovering Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing exactly.<tbc>

• **Diverse Shortest Cycles.** Taking \(\ell=0\) removes the coverage requirement, leaving the problem of finding _k_ shortest cycles that are pairwise _d_-diverse. This fits within the growing literature on _diversity_ in combinatorial optimization \[2, 15, 17\]: rather than a single optimal solution, one seeks a collection of near-optimal solutions that are spread out in a meaningful<tbc>

_Task:_ & Decide whether there exists a set C={_C_<sub>1</sub>_,C_<sub>2</sub>_,...,C<sub>k</sub>_} of exactly _k_ many pairwise _d_-diverse shortest cycles of _G_ such that the weight of the set of edges covered by these cycles is at least \(\ell\), that is, \(w\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kE(C_i)\right)\ge\ell\). \\

sense. On planar graphs, _d_-diversity among shortest cycles translates directly to _d_-diversity among global minimum cuts in the dual graph, connecting our result to the work of de Berg, Martínez, and Spieksma \[7\] on diverse minimum _s-t_ cuts.<tbc>

• **Maximum Edge Coverage by Shortest Cycles.** Taking _d=w(E(G_)) removes the diversity requirement, leaving the problem of finding _k_ shortest cycles whose union covers edges of total weight as large as possible. This can be seen as a variant of the classical Maximum Coverage problem (find _k_ sets from a family S covering the most elements) with the important distinction that S is not given explicitly: the family of all shortest cycles of _G_ can be exponentially large and given implicitly rather than enumerated.

Our main algorithmic result not only resolves the open question from \[3\] asking for a single- exponential algorithm for Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing on planar graphs, but also establishes the first FPT algorithms for Diverse Shortest Cycles and Maximum Edge Coverage by Shortest Cycles on planar graphs.

**Theorem 1.2.** Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage _on planar graphs admits an algorithm with running time_ \(2^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\).

The running time in Theorem 1.2 is stated assuming the word RAM model. We note that the result holds for real-valued edge weights assuming the standard real RAM model of computation, in which basic arithmetic operations on real numbers can be performed in constant time.

## 1.1 Related Work

Both Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing and Vertex-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing are NP-complete even on planar graphs, since they generalize the triangle packing problem \[4, 3\]. Rautenbach and Regen \[24\] studied these problems on graphs of girth \(g\in\{4,5\}\). In this case, both problems are solvable in polynomial time on graphs of maximum degree 3, but are APX-hard for maximum degree 4. For \(g\ge 6\), the problems are APX-hard already on cubic graphs. Approximation algorithms of ratio \((3+\varepsilon)\) for Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing and Vertex-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing on planar graphs follow from the framework of Schlomberg, Thiele, and Vygen \[26\] for uncrossing families of cycles.

The systematic parameterized study of Vertex-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing and Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing was initiated in \[4, 3\]. For general graphs, they gave an XP algorithm with running time _n_<sup>O(_k_<sup>6</sup>)</sup>, which constituted the first algorithm solving these problems for any fixed _k_, and ruled out a polynomial kernel under standard complexity assumptions. The FPT vs. W\[1\]-hard status of Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing and Vertex-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing on general graphs was left explicitly open. For planar graphs, they obtained a polynomial kernel with O(_k_<sup>2</sup>) vertices and an FPT algorithm with running time \(k^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\), and explicitly asked whether a single-exponential algorithm exists. Our Theorem 1.1 resolves the first open question by proving W\[1\]-hardness on subcubic graphs, and Theorem 1.2 resolves the second by giving a \(2^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\) algorithm for the more general Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage on planar graphs.

A close relative of shortest cycle packing is Disjoint Shortest Paths. In this problem, given _k_ pairs of terminal vertices, the task is to decide whether they can be connected by pairwise vertex- (or edge-) disjoint shortest paths. The problem is NP-hard when _k_ is part of the input \[13\] and<tbc>

<tbc>W[1]-hard parameterized by _k_ [5]. Lochet [21] gave a polynomial-time algorithm for any fixed _k_ in undirected unweighted graphs, with an improved running time obtained in [5]. The recent breakthrough of Pilipczuk, Stamoulis, and Włodarczyk [23] establishes that the problem is FPT on planar graphs.

In our paper, we are using laminar shortest cycles trees introduced in [4, 3]; similar laminar structures of cycles in planar graphs have been use before [18, 16, 26, 25].

There has been growing interest in finding _diverse_ collections of solutions to combinatorial optimization problems from the perspective of parameterized complexity. The paper [2] initiated this line of research, and [15] developed a general framework for diverse collections in matroids and graphs. Eiben, Koana, and Wahlström [12] developed algebraic techniques based on determinantal sieving that apply to various problems in the diverse-solutions settings, although their methods are not applicable to our problem. Other general techniques were recently proposed by Kumabe [20] and Ashok et al. [1]. However, our problem does not fit into this framework as in our case, the diversity measures and the size of the diverse objects (that is, the girth) are unbounded. In the context of cuts, the papers [7, 8] studied diverse minimum _s-t_ cuts and diverse solutions in problems with a distributive lattice structure. More recently [9] gave an FPT algorithm for finding diverse minimum _s-t_ cuts. Our problem Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage contributes to this line of work, where the objects of interest are shortest cycles and diversity is measured by the weight of pairwise edge intersections; on planar graphs, this is equivalent to diversity among global minimum cuts in the dual graph.

## 2 Overview of our methods

### 2.1 Proof of Theorem 1.1

The reduction in [4] establishes W[1]-hardness of deciding, given a graph _G_ and integers _k_ and _L_, whether _G_ contains _k_ vertex- (or edge-) disjoint cycles of length at most _L_ each. In this reduction, _L_ may be larger than the girth of _G_, and this flexibility is crucial. In the case of shortest cycles, however, all cycles must have length exactly equal to the girth of _G_. This tight length constraint requires substantially more intricate arguments, even though we reuse some ideas from [4].

Theorem 1.1 is proved by reducing from the W[1]-hard Multicolored Clique problem. This problem asks, given a graph _G_ whose vertices are partitioned into _h_ sets _V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>h</sub>_, called _color classes_, whether _G_ has a _multicolored_ clique of size _h_, that is, a clique containing exactly one vertex from each color class. The parameter of Multicolored Clique is the size of the solution size _h_. The key ingredients of our reduction are the constructions of _vertex_ and _edge_ selection gadgets which are used to encode the selection of exactly one vertex in each color class and exactly one edge between every pair of color classes of the input instance of Multicolored Clique. Then we combine these gadgets to encode the instance of Multicolored Clique. To construct vertex and edge selection gadgets, we select a sufficiently large (with respect to the size of _G_) integer \(L=2\ell\) which will be the girth of the constructed graph, and then build gadgets as unions of overlapping packings of cycles of length _L_.

The crucial difference between the W[1]-hardness proof in [4] and our result is that the edge selection gadget allows us to work with shortest cycles, while [4] has to relax the length constraint. For the edge selection gadget _F_, we assume that the number of edges between each pair of color classes is the same integer _m_. Then _F_ contains _m_ 4-tuples of _L_-length cycles. The idea is demonstrated<tbc>

The crucial property of the gadget is that if we wish to take 4 edge-disjoint shortest cycles from _F_, then because of the overlap of the shortest cycles, the only option is to choose cycles of the same color. This choice corresponds to the selection of an edge in the instance of Multicolored Clique between two color classes.

The construction of the vertex selection gadget _H_ exploits the same idea. We assume that each color class contains _n_ vertices. Then _H_ is composed of _n_ pairs of cycles of length _L_. To see the idea, notice that the selection of, say, the red cycles in the vertex selection gadget in Figure 2 leaves the edges of _Q_<sub>1</sub> free to use in other cycles in the attached edge selection gadgets. We apply this idea to argue that _G_ has a multicolored clique if and only if the constructed graph has a packing of \(2h+4\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) edge-disjoint shortest cycles.

Let us highlight the aspects of the reduction that we consider the most delicate. First, since every cycle of the packing must have length exactly \(g(G')=L\), all gadgets are built as unions of overlapping cycles of length exactly _L_, and their correctness rests on an overlap argument: the 4-tuples of shortest cycles in an edge selection gadget (the pairs of shortest cycles in an vertex selection gadget) share edges in a cyclically shifted pattern, which forces a monochromatic choice. Second, the gadgets are glued together by identifying root edges of edge selection gadgets with specific edges of vertex selection gadgets. Each identification creates new cycles passing through several gadgets, and we must certify that none of them has length below _L_. Finally, the equivalence rests on an exact counting argument: the budget \(k=2h+4\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) equals the maximum number of edge-disjoint shortest cycles that the gadgets can jointly supply, so every gadget must be saturated, and saturation is possible only along a selection encoding a multicolored clique.

## 2.2 Proof of Theorem 1.2

We give an intuitive idea behind our algorithm that proves Theorem 1.2. At a high level, our algorithm has two sources of novelty compared to the \(k^{\mathcal{O}(k)}\cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\)-time algorithm of \[4\]: a finer structural analysis of the laminar shortest cycles tree, which reduces all guessing from quadratically many objects to linearly many, and a new two-layer dynamic programming.

Consider an instance \((G,w,k,d,\ell)\) of Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage, where _G_ is a planar graph. We assume that every edge of _G_ is in some shortest cycle, and _G_ is embedded on the plane in such a way that the frontier of the external (outer) face is a shortest cycle. Whenever we say that _G_ is a plane graph, we mean that _G_ is embedded this way. The work \[4\] introduces a tree-like structure that captures the shortest cycles in a weighted plane graph, called the _laminar shortest cycles tree (LSCT)_; similar structures have also been previously used (for instance, see \[18, 26, 16, 25\]). Intuitively speaking, a family of shortest cycles C in a given plane graph _G_ is _laminar_ if for distinct \(C,C'\in\mathcal{C}\), one of the following holds: i) _C_ is drawn inside \(C'\), ii) \(C'\) is drawn inside _C_, or iii) the regions (not containing the outer face) bounded by the closed curves of _C_ and \(C'\) are disjoint.

We begin by computing the laminar shortest cycles tree T for the given plane graph _G_ (see Definition 5.4 for the formal definition). The nodes of this tree are shortest cycles in _G_ (but not all of them). Figure 3 illustrates the kind of shortest cycles that are missing from T ; an intuitive explanation follows below. The only shortest cycles in _G_ that are not nodes of T are those consisting of two "non-consecutive" shortest paths, each of length _g(G)/_2, between a pair of vertices \(s,t\in V(G)\), where _g(G_) is the weighted girth of _G_; moreover, such a pair excludes the two "outermost" shortest _s-t_ paths. The shortest cycles that are nodes of T are _tree cycles_ and the ones that are not its nodes are _non-tree cycles_.

We briefly describe the construction of this laminar shortest cycles tree, since its properties will be algorithmically exploited. Intuitively, the tree is rooted at this outer face shortest cycle, and we (recursively) add shortest cycles to this tree by going "inside" the region (not containing the outer face) bounded by the current shortest cycle node \(\alpha\) as follows. (See Figure 4 for an illustrative example; the concrete details in the figure relate to the formal definition presented later and may be ignored at this point.) Find a maximal set C of shortest cycles where i) each of them is fully<tbc>

<tbc>contained inside \(\alpha\) in the given planar drawing, ii) no shortest cycle in C fully contains another shortest cycle from C in the planar drawing, and iii) there is no cycle (different from \(\alpha\)) contained inside \(\alpha\) that fully contains a cycle from C. We make each \(\beta\in\mathscr{C}\) a child of \(\alpha\), and recursively proceed until we reach facial cycles. Roughly speaking, the above gives a clean "laminar" structure of shortest cycles in the given plane graph, and one may think of it as encountering cycles "layer- by-layer" starting from the outermost cycle.

## A simpler case of edge-disjoint cycles.

The work \[4\] uses the laminar shortest cycles tree to obtain an FPT algorithm for Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing, running in time \(k^{O(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}\), for the given plane graph _G_ as follows: i) if the number of leaves in the laminar shortest cycles tree T is at least 4_k_, using the Four Color Theorem, one can directly conclude that the instance is a yes-instance. ii) Else, the number of leaves in T is less than 4_k_. In this case, they show that there is a set of _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) appropriately selected "deepest" (in the layers) shortest cycles which necessarily contains a solution (if one exists). We remark that the above marking scheme relies on the "strict laminarity" property of some optimal solution; we discuss strict laminarity in more detail shortly. With these marked cycles, now one can easily obtain an FPT algorithm running in time \(k^{O(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}\).

Again, the non-trivial case for us is when the number of leaves in the laminar shortest cycles tree T for the given plane graph _G_ is less than 4_k_. It remains to handle the tree cycles, which are exactly the nodes of the laminar shortest cycles tree T . We proceed by a bottom-up dynamic programming over T , starting from its leaves, as follows. At a node \(\alpha\) of T , we seek a solution that contains \(\alpha\) and some descendants of \(\alpha\), and we assume that for every strict descendant of \(\alpha\) the corresponding dynamic programming entries have already been computed. We note that the number of nodes in T may not be bounded by a function of _k_, and thus we do not know which descendants to query directly. However, as the number of leaves in T is bounded, so is the number of nodes of degree at least 3, as well as the number of inclusion-maximal paths in T containing only nodes of degree 2. So intuitively, we can guess whether the "closest" descendant of \(\alpha\) in the solution is a leaf, a node of degree at least three, or a node lying on a maximal degree-2 path (and how many solution cycles appear below it).

Once we have the above information (the number of possible guesses is 2<sup>O(_k_)</sup>), we know precisely the descendants that are leaves or nodes of degree at least three, and the unknown ones lie on maximal degree-2 paths. **Handling the general case of Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage.** The algorithmic steps we discussed for Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing up to the greedy choice handling descendants on maximal degree-2 paths of T , remain the same. However, as the strict laminarity property completely breaks down when cycles can share edges, the greedy strategy does not work. More precisely, two cycles in different maximal degree-2 paths may intersect and the greedy strategy falls apart. Instead, our approach is to handle the choices of descendants across different maximal degree-2 paths simultaneously, in one go. To achieve this, we need a better understanding of the structure of the solution we are looking for, as we explain next.

Let \(\alpha\) be a node of T and let the "closest" tree cycles in an optimal solution that appear "below" \(\alpha\) in T be the unknown cycles \(\beta_1,\beta_2,\cdots,\beta_b\). In the above, by "closest" we mean that there is no tree cycle in the solution that is strictly between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta_i\), \(i\in[b]\). Recall that we cannot precisely guess the \(\beta_i\)s that belong to maximal degree 2 paths. Let us take a closer look at the "unknown" cycle \(\beta_i\), which belongs to a maximal degree 2 path _Q_ in the subtree \(\mathcal{T}_\alpha\) of T rooted at \(\alpha\). Furthermore, let \(\gamma_i\) be the endpoint of _Q_ that is closest to \(\alpha\). Using planarity, we can guarantee that the edges that \(\beta_i\) may share with some \(\beta_j\), where \(j\in[b]\backslash\{i\}\) must also belong to \(\gamma_i\) (see Figure 5) and such intersections are highly structured, as illustrated in the figure.

Also, by the structure of intersections of shortest cycles, we can guarantee that \(P_i=\gamma_i\cap\beta_i\) is a sub-path of \(\gamma_i\). These two properties let us completely identify the "non-trivial" part of the intersection of \(\beta_i\) with other cycles once we know, roughly speaking, the "start" and "end" cycle intersections lying on _P<sub>i</sub>_. Thus, we will use the above information to derive the solution we are looking for. At the above step, we will again exploit planarity to ensure that we can achieve the above in time \(2^{O(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}\). We remark that only "start" and "end" cycles are relevant for \(\beta_i\). We encode these guessed "end-cycles" as a graph, in which we can guarantee that each connected component is a path or a cycle. These highly structured components then allow us to identify the correct solution descendants by a second, separate dynamic programming.

Let us highlight the aspects of the algorithm that we consider the most novel. First, the marking scheme of \[4\] inherently costs _k_<sup>O(_k_)</sup>: it identifies O(_k_<sup>2</sup>) candidate cycles and guesses the solution among them. To obtain a single-exponential running time, every guess in our algorithm must range over objects whose number is linear in _k_ (the longitudinal paths covering the non-tree cycles, the marked representatives, and the intersection types) and it is planarity that keeps the product of all these choices single-exponential: a sparsity argument in the dual graph shows that the total size of the "relevant sets" of all representatives is linear in their number, so that the intersection types can be enumerated in 2<sup>O(_k_)</sup> time overall. Second, for _d\>_0 the strict laminarity property, on which the approach of \[4\] (as well as our simpler algorithm for the edge-disjoint case) crucially relies, completely breaks down: an optimal solution may be forced to use cycles that pairwise share edges, and the choices of solution descendants on different maximal degree-2 paths of T interact through these shared edges. Our replacement for the greedy step is a second layer of dynamic programming: the guessed "start" and "end" intersections define an auxiliary graph whose connected components are paths and cycles, and the interactions within each component are resolved by a dynamic program along it. Finally, the coverage objective introduces a difficulty absent from pure packing: the algorithm must account exactly for the weight of edges covered by two solution cycles, including cycles it never explicitly identifies. The structured intersections in planar graphs (no edge belongs to three solution cycles, and the pairwise intersections are subpaths of the known representatives) are precisely what makes this bookkeeping possible.

## 3 Preliminaries

**Numbers and Sets.** We denote the set of natural numbers by N={0,1,2_,..._}. For \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), we use \[_p_\] to denote the set {1_,...,p_}. The set of integers is denoted by Z, and \(\mathbb{Z}_{>0}=\{a\in\mathbb{Z}|a>0\}\). We will use the following folklore result, which can be obtained using the well-known AM-GM inequality.

**Proposition 3.1.** _For_ \(z,z_1,z_2,\cdots,z_\ell\in\mathbb{N}\)_, where_ \(z=\sum_{i\in[\ell]}z_i\)_, we have_ \(\prod_{i\in[\ell]}z_i\in 2^{O(z)}\).

**Graphs & weighted graphs.** Throughout this paper, we consider finite undirected graphs and refer to the textbook of Diestel \[10\] for any undefined graph-theoretic notions. Unless stated otherwise, all graphs are simple.

For a graph _G_, _V(G_) and _E(G_) denote the vertex set and the edge set of _G_, respectively. We denote the number of vertices and edges of _G_ by _n_ and _m_, respectively. A graph together with an edge-weight function \(w:E(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) is a _weighted graph_. Unless stated otherwise, whenever we write weighted graph, we will mean an edge weighted graph. For \(U\subseteq V(G)\), we write _G_\[_U_\] for the subgraph of _G_ induced by _U_, i.e., _V(G_\[_U_\])=_U_ and \(E(G[U])=\{\{u,v\}\in E(G)|u,v\in U\}\). For two graphs _G_<sub>1</sub> and _G_<sub>2</sub>, their _intersection_ is the graph \(G_1\cap G_2\) with \(V(G_1\cap G_2)=V(G_1)\cap V(G_2)\) and \(E(G_1\cap G_2)=E(G_1)\cap E(G_2)\), while their _union_ \(G_1\cup G_2\) is the graph with \(V(G_1\cup G_2)=V(G_1)\cup V(G_2)\) and \(E(G_1\cup G_2)=E(G_1)\cup E(G_2)\).

Consider a weighted graph _G_ with \(w:E(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\). For \(X\subseteq E(G)\), \(w(X)=\sum_{e\in X}w(e)\). For a subgraph _H_ of _G_, _w(H_)=_w(E(H_)). An ordered sequence of distinct vertices _P_=(_u_<sub>1</sub>=_u,u_<sub>2</sub>_,...,u<sub>\</sub>=v_) is a _path_ in _G_ between vertices _u_ and _v_ if \(\{u_i,u_{i+1}\}\in E(G)\) for all \(1\le i\le\ell-1\). We use the notation _P(u,v_) to denote a path between two vertices _u,v_; alternatively we say that _P_ is a _u-v_ path. The vertices _u_<sub>1</sub> and \(u_\ell\) are the _endpoints_ of _P_, and the remaining vertices are its _internal_ vertices. A _subpath_ of _P_ is any path of the form (_u<sub>i</sub>,u_<sub>_i_+1</sub>_,...,u<sub>j</sub>_) for \(1\le i\le j\le\ell\). The length of a path is defined as the sum of the weights of edges of the path, i.e., \(w(P)=\sum_{i\in[l-1]}w(\{u_i,u_{i+1}\})\). For two vertices _u_ and _v_ of _G_, the distance between them is the length of the shortest path between them. A _cycle_ is a path along with an additional edge between the two endpoints of the path. The _length_ of a cycle is the sum of the weights of its edges. A _shortest cycle_ of a graph is the smallest length cycle. The _girth_, _g(G_), is the minimum-weight of a cycle in _G_, i.e. _g(G_)=min{_w(C_)|_C_ is a cycle in _G_}. We say that the graph _G_ is _clean_ if every edge and vertex belongs to some shortest cycle.

**Planar graphs.** A graph is _planar_ if we can draw it on a plane without any pair of edges crossing (except at the shared endpoint, if any), and such a drawing is called a _planar embedding_ of the graph. We can find a planar embedding of a planar graph in linear time \[19\]. A planar graph _G_ with a fixed embedding on the plane is a _plane_ graph. The _faces_ of a plane graph are the open regions of the plane bounded by edges and containing no vertices or edges in their interior. The outer region is the _external_ face, and the other faces are _internal_. The vertices and edges appearing on the closed walk bounding a face form its _frontier_. A cycle _C_ of _G_ is called a _facial cycle_ if it is the frontier of some face.

For a shortest cycle _C_ of a plane graph _G_, we denote by _G<sub>C</sub>_ the subgraph of _G_ induced by the vertices lying on _C_ or in the interior Int(_C_) of the region bounded by the curve of _C_ in the plane. (In the above by interior region, we mean the region not containing the outer face.) For the two shortest cycles _C_<sub>1</sub> and _C_<sub>2</sub> in the plane graph _G_, we say \(C_1\le C_2\) if every vertex and edge of _C_<sub>1</sub> is either a vertex or edge of _C_<sub>2</sub> or is embedded in the curve of _C_<sub>2</sub>, i.e., Int(_C_<sub>2</sub>).

The _dual_ graph of a plane graph _G_, denoted _G_<sup>∗</sup>=(_F(G),E_<sup>∗</sup>), has one vertex for each face of _G_. For every edge \(e\in E(G)\), there is a corresponding _dual_ edge \(e^*\in E^*\) whose endpoints are the two faces whose frontiers contain _e_; if _e_ lies on the frontier of exactly one face (i.e., _e_ is a bridge), then _e_<sup>∗</sup> is a self-loop at that face. Note that _G_<sup>∗</sup> need not be simple even if _G_ is simple.

**Parameterized Complexity.** We refer to the textbooks by Cygan et al. \[6\] and by Downey and Fellows \[11\] for a comprehensive introduction to parameterized complexity. Here, we briefly recall the main definitions.

A _parameterized problem_ is a language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb{N}\), where \(\Sigma^*\) denotes the set of finite strings<tbc>

<tbc>over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\). An instance of _L_ is a pair (_x,k_), where \(x\in\Sigma^*\) is the input and \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) is the _parameter_. A parameterized problem is _fixed-parameter tractable_ (FPT, for short) if it can be solved in time \(f(k)\cdot|x|^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\) for some computable function _f_. The class FPT consists of all fixed-parameter tractable parameterized problems.

For two parameterized problems \(A,B\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\mathbb{N}\), a _parameterized reduction_ from _A_ to _B_ is an algorithm which given an instance (_x,k_) of _A_ produces an equivalent instance \((x',k')\) of _B_ in time \(f(k)\cdot|x|^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\) and the parameter \(k'\le g(k)\) for some computable functions _f_ and _g_.

The standard approach to ruling out the existence of an FPT-algorithm for a parameterized problem, under the standard assumptions in parameterized complexity that \(\mathsf{FPT}\neq W[1]\), is to prove that the problem is _W_\[1\]_-hard_. In particular, if there exists a _parameterized reduction_ from a _W_\[1\]-hard parameterized problem _A_ to a parameterized problem _B_, then _B_ is also _W_\[1\]-hard.

Assume that _R_ contains vertices of one vertex selection gadget _H<sub>i</sub>_ for some \(i\in[h]\). Then _R_ contains vertices of one edge selection gadget _F<sub>i,j</sub>_ for some \(j\in[h]\). As \(E(R)\backslash E(H_i)\neq\emptyset\) and \(E(R)\backslash E(F_{i,j})\neq\emptyset\), _R_ is the union of edge-disjoint paths in _H<sub>i</sub>_ and _F<sub>i,j</sub>_, and the endpoints of these paths in _F<sub>i,j</sub>_ are the endpoints of the root edges identified with slot edges of _H<sub>i</sub>_. If _R_ has two edge-disjoint paths whose endpoints are endpoints of distinct root edges of _F<sub>i,j</sub>_, the length of _R_ is at least 2(_L_-2_m_+1)_\>L_ by Claim (ii) of Lemma 4.1. Suppose that _R_ contains one path in _F<sub>i,j</sub>_ whose endpoints are endpoints of distinct root edges. Then _R_ is the union of this paths and a path _H<sub>i</sub>_ with the same endpoints. By Claims (ii) of Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.2, the length of _R_ is at least (_L_-2_m_+1)+2_m\>L_. This finishes the case analysis and proves that the length of _R_ is at least _L_+1.

Now we are ready to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1 by showing that the instance (_G,V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>h</sub>_) of Multicolored Clique is equivalent to the constructed instance \((G',k)\) of Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing.

**Lemma 4.4.** _The graph G has a multicolored clique if and only if_ \(G'\) _has a packing of k edge-disjoint shortest cycles._

_Proof._ Suppose that \(\{x_{i_1}^1,\dots,x_{i_h}^h\}\) is a clique of _G_. We construct the packing P of edge-disjoint shortest cycles of \(G'\) as follows. Recall that \(g(G')=L\) by Lemma 4.3. We construct P by using packings of cycles of length _L_ in the vertex and edge selection gadgets. By Claim (v) of Lemma 4.2, for each \(j\in[h]\), there is a packing of two edge-disjoint cycles in _H<sub>j</sub>_ such that the slots of \(S_{i_j}^j\) are free. We include in P these cycles. Consider arbitrary \(j,r\in[h]\) such that _j\<r_. Because \(x_{i_j}^j\) and \(x_{i_r}^r\) are adjacent in _G_, by the construction of \(G'\), there is a pair of two opposite root edges _e<sub>t</sub>_ and \(e'_t\) of _F<sub>j,r</sub>_ such that _e<sub>t</sub>_ is identified with an edge of \(S_{i_j}^j\) and \(e'_t\) is identified with an edge of \(S_{i_r}^r\). By Claim (v) of Lemma 4.1, _F<sub>j,r</sub>_ has a packing of four edge-disjoint shortest cycles that have common edges only with the slot edges of \(S_{i_j}^j\) and \(S_{i_r}^r\), and do not contain other slot edges of _H<sub>j</sub>_ and _H<sub>r</sub>_, then we take these four cycles in P. By doing this for all pairs \(j,r\in[h]\) such that _j\<r_, we obtain P that contains \(2h+4\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}=k\) edge-disjoint shortest cycles.

For the opposite direction, suppose that \(G'\) has a packing of \(k=2h+4\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\) edge-disjoint shortest cycles. By the second claim of Lemma 4.3, each shortest cycle of \(G'\) is a shortest cycle of either a vertex or an edge selection gadget. By Claims (iv) of Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.2, each vertex selection gadget contains at most two edge-disjoint shortest cycles, and each edge selection gadget contains at most four edge-disjoint shortest cycles. Since P is of size \(2h+4\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\), P contains exactly two cycles from each vertex selection gadget and exactly four cycles from each edge selection gadget. By Claim (v) of Lemma 4.2, for each \(j\in[h]\), there is a unique \(i_j\in[n]\) such that \(S_{i_j}^j\) contains free slots with respect to P. We claim that \(\{x_{i_1}^1,\dots,x_{i_h}^h\}\) is a clique of _G_.

To show the claim, consider arbitrary \(j,r\in[h]\) such that _j\<r_. We prove that \(x_jx_r\in E(G)\). To see this, recall that _F<sub>j,r</sub>_ contains four edge-disjoint shortest cycles from P. By Claim (v) of Lemma 4.1, there is a unique \(t\in[m]\) such that the opposite roots \(e_t,e'_t\) of _F<sub>j,r</sub>_ are in the cycles of the packing P, and all other roots are not included in the cycles. This implies that _e<sub>t</sub>_ and \(e'_t\) are identified with the free slots of _H<sub>j</sub>_ and _H<sub>r</sub>_. Since only \(S_{i_j}^j\) and \(S_{i_r}^r\) contain free slots, we have that _e<sub>t</sub>_ is identified with an edge of \(S_{i_j}^j\), and \(e'_t\) is identified with an edge of \(S_{i_r}^r\). Since _e<sub>t</sub>_ and \(e'_t\) are opposite roots of _F<sub>j,r</sub>_, this means that _G_ contains the edge \(x_{i_j}^jx_{i_r}^r\). Because \(j,r\in[h]\) are arbitrary, we have that the vertices of \(\{x_{i_1}^1,\dots,x_{i_h}^h\}\) are pairwise adjacent, that is, they form a multicolored clique. This concludes the proof.

Taking into account that \(G'\) can be constructed in polynomial time and \(k=2h+4\genfrac(){pt}{2}{h}{2}\), Lemma 4.4 proves Theorem 1.1.

We have proved Lemma 5.6, which completes the proof of Lemma 5.5, which in turn finishes the proof of Theorem 1.2. ## 6 Conclusion and Open Questions In this paper we resolved two open questions from \[4, 3\] on packing shortest cycles. First, we showed that Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing is W\[1\]-hard parameterized by _k_ already on unweighted subcubic graphs, ruling out FPT algorithms for the problem on general graphs. Second, we obtained a single-exponential algorithm for Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage on planar graphs. Several questions remain open. **Kernelization.** First, does Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage admit a polynomial-in-_k_ kernel on planar graphs? We are able to establish kernelization for some special cases, but the general case remains open. More precisely, for planar graphs, \[4, 3\] show that Edge-Disjoint

Shortest Cycle Packing admits a kernel with O(_k_<sup>2</sup>) vertices. By making use of a very similar approach, we are able to show that the special case of Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage without constraints on covering \(\ell\) -- that is, the task of finding _k d_-diverse shortest cycles -- admits a kernel with O(_k_<sup>2</sup>) vertices on planar graphs. However, we could not obtain a similar result for the coverage variant, even without constraints on diversity; that is, the problem of finding _k_ shortest cycles covering the edge set of maximum total weight. Obtaining a polynomial kernel for coverage problem on planar graphs is the first natural step towards the kernel for Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage.

**Subexponential algorithms.** Many cycle- and packing-related problems on planar graphs admit subexponential-time algorithms, yet we do not know whether this holds for problems around packing of shortest cycles. Proving a lower bound that rules out \(2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}\) algorithms under ETH, or obtaining a subexponential algorithm for Diverse Shortest Cycle Coverage and Edge- Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing is another interesting open question.

**Sparse classes of graphs.** We establish that Edge-Disjoint Shortest Cycle Packing is W[1]-hard even on subcubic graphs, so the problem remains intractable on sparse graphs in general. However, it is plausible that the problem could be FPT on sparse graphs of specific structure, such as _H_-minor-free graphs or graphs of bounded expansion. Our methods are tailored to planar graphs, and different techniques would most likely be needed here.
